mcqs.question: A page's median LCP is 1.9s but its 75th-percentile LCP is 3.4s. How is the URL assessed?
options: Needs improvement — assessment uses the 75th percentile, which is between 2.5s and 4.0s
Good — the median is comfortably under the 2.5s threshold
Poor — any percentile above 2.5s fails the metric outright
Good, provided the other two vitals are also good at the median
mcqs.explanation: Core Web Vitals are assessed at the 75th percentile of real visits, so 3.4s lands in the needs-improvement band regardless of a healthy median. Optimising the median is exactly the trap the percentile rule is designed to close, and 3.4s is not poor either — that band starts above 4.0s.

mcqs.question: During load, a heading paints at 0.9s and a larger hero image paints at 2.2s. What is reported as LCP?
options: 0.9s — the first contentful element becomes the LCP candidate and is locked in
The average of the two candidate times, 1.55s
2.2s — the candidate updates as larger elements render, and finalises at the first interaction
Both are reported separately, one per candidate element
mcqs.explanation: LCP tracks the largest contentful element seen so far and keeps updating as bigger candidates paint, freezing at the first user interaction — so the hero image supersedes the heading. Nothing is averaged, and only a single value is reported per page load.

mcqs.question: A button's click handler starts within 4ms but the UI takes 700ms to visibly update. How do FID and INP score this?
options: Both score it poorly, since both measure end-to-end interaction latency
FID scores it as excellent because it only measures input delay; INP scores it as poor because it measures through to the next paint
FID scores it poorly and INP scores it well, since INP excludes rendering time
Neither applies, because button clicks are excluded from both metrics
mcqs.explanation: FID stopped the clock when the handler began, so a 4ms start looked perfect no matter how long the response took — precisely the blind spot that led to INP replacing it in March 2024. INP spans input delay, processing, and presentation delay, so the 700ms render is fully counted.

mcqs.question: An element covering half the viewport shifts downward by a quarter of the viewport height. Roughly what layout shift score does that contribute?
options: 0.125 — impact fraction times distance fraction
0.75 — impact fraction plus distance fraction
0.25 — the distance fraction alone determines the score
0.5 — the impact fraction alone determines the score
mcqs.explanation: The score is impact fraction multiplied by distance fraction, so 0.5 × 0.25 = 0.125 — enough on its own to exceed the 0.1 good threshold. Using either fraction alone, or adding them, badly overstates or understates how much a shift actually hurts.

mcqs.question: Your CLS is driven mainly by a web font swapping in and changing text height. Which fix targets the cause most directly?
options: Switch the font declaration to `font-display: swap` so the text appears sooner
Move the font file to a CDN to shorten its download time
Lazy-load the font so it never competes with the hero image
Use `size-adjust` and `ascent-override` so the fallback font occupies the same space as the web font
mcqs.explanation: The shift comes from the fallback and web font having different metrics, so overriding the fallback's metrics makes the swap cause no reflow at all — the only fix that addresses the actual cause. `font-display: swap` explicitly permits the swap that causes the shift, and shortening download time only makes the shift happen earlier rather than removing it.

mcqs.question: Lighthouse gives a page 97 and reports CLS of 0.01, but CrUX shows CLS at 0.31. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Lighthouse measures CLS over a longer window than the field, so it dilutes individual shifts
Real users scroll into lazy-loaded content, ads, and consent banners that a default Lighthouse run never triggers
CrUX reports the maximum CLS across all visits rather than a percentile
The two use different formulas, since CrUX includes shifts caused by user interaction
mcqs.explanation: A lab run loads the page once, without scrolling or consent flows, so the shifts that dominate real sessions simply never happen — this is the standard cause of a near-zero lab CLS against a failing field value. CrUX reports the 75th percentile, and both use the same formula, which explicitly excludes shifts within 500ms of an interaction.
